subject: Climate & Environment
title: Urban Heat Islands
description: Learn Urban Heat Islands in one minute.

hook.text: Cities can be 5 to 10°C hotter than surrounding countryside on summer nights.

buildup.text: Concrete, asphalt, and buildings absorb heat all day and radiate it back at night.

discovery.text: Few trees and little vegetation mean less shade and less cooling through evaporation.

twist.text: Air conditioning pumps indoor heat outdoors — making streets even hotter in a feedback loop.

climax.text: Painting roofs white and planting urban forests can drop temperatures by several degrees.

punchline.text: Cities built to keep weather out are now trapping heat in.

quiz.question: What causes the urban heat island effect?
options: Concrete and asphalt absorb and radiate heat
People generate body heat in dense crowds

details.summary: Urban heat islands form because cities replace vegetation with pavement, buildings, and asphalt that absorb and re-radiate heat. Cities can be 5 to 12 degrees warmer than surrounding rural areas, amplifying heat wave danger for the billions living in urban environments.
details.whyItMatters: As urbanization and warming grow simultaneously, heat islands will push urban temperatures to deadly levels far exceeding regional averages.
takeaways: Cities can be 5 to 12 degrees warmer than surrounding rural areas
Dark surfaces like asphalt absorb up to 95 percent of solar radiation
Green infrastructure and cool roofs can reduce urban temperatures by 2 to 5 degrees

faq.question: Why are urban heat islands worse at night?
faq.answer: Building materials absorb solar heat during the day and release it slowly at night, preventing the cooling that naturally occurs in vegetated areas. This nighttime heat is especially dangerous because the body needs cooler nights to recover from daytime heat stress.

faq.question: What can cities do to reduce heat islands?
faq.answer: Planting urban trees, installing cool or green roofs, using reflective pavements, and creating parks all reduce heat absorption and increase cooling. Some cities mandate cool-roof standards and fund tree planting in the hottest neighborhoods.
